_note: Quote of the day (/conhecimentos/citacoes). Portuguese-language quotations only, by authors who died before 1956, so their work is in the public domain in Portugal and the EU (life + 70 years). Mostly Portugal; Machado de Assis and Olavo Bilac (Brazil) are marked as Brazilian in `place` and `bio`. Living or recently dead authors (José Saramago, Sophia de Mello Breyner Andresen, Miguel Torga, Eugénio de Andrade, José Régio, Cecília Meireles, Clarice Lispector, Carlos Drummond de Andrade …) are left out because their work is still protected. Every quote is a line from the author's own work and `source` names that work; Pessoa's heteronyms (Alberto Caeiro, Ricardo Reis, Álvaro de Campos, Bernardo Soares) are named in `source`, the author stays Pessoa. `year` is the year of first publication, unless it says otherwise. Spelling is modern European Portuguese (Acordo Ortográfico de 1990) for every author. Left out on purpose: lines often attributed but not from the author's work (“Os políticos e as fraldas devem ser mudados…” is not Eça; “Pedras no caminho? Guardo todas…” and “O valor das coisas não está no tempo que elas duram…” are not Pessoa) and “Navegar é preciso; viver não é preciso”, which Pessoa quotes as an old sailors' saying (from Plutarch's Latin) rather than as his own line. Verse line breaks are ' / ' (oneLine() in zitateData.js turns them into spaces). `disputed: true` would show a badge; no quote needs it. `meaning` says the quote in plain English (A2–B1). Word fields keep their old names: `de` is the Portuguese word, `art` o or a. Written 2026-11-21 (culture run) from memory of the works, not checked against an edition; see the to-verify list in the culture report.

camoes.name: Luís de Camões
camoes.bio: Camões wrote Os Lusíadas, the national epic of Portugal, about Vasco da Gama's voyage to India. He lived as a soldier in North Africa and Asia and lost an eye in battle. Portugal's national day, 10 June, is the day of his death, and Portuguese is sometimes called “the language of Camões”.

vieira.name: Padre António Vieira
vieira.bio: Vieira was a Jesuit priest who spent much of his life in Brazil. His sermons are classics of Portuguese prose. He defended the Indigenous peoples of Brazil, and he was put on trial by the Inquisition.

garrett.name: Almeida Garrett
garrett.bio: Garrett brought Romanticism to Portugal. He wrote poems, plays and the travel book Viagens na Minha Terra, and he helped to found the national theatre in Lisbon. As a liberal he spent years in exile.

camilo.name: Camilo Castelo Branco
camilo.bio: Camilo wrote more than a hundred books. His best-known novel, Amor de Perdição, was written in the Porto prison, where he was held for a love affair. His own life was as dramatic as his novels.

antero.name: Antero de Quental
antero.bio: Antero was born in the Azores. He is known for his sonnets, which ask big questions about life, faith and death. He was also active in politics and in the first workers' movements in Portugal.

eca.name: Eça de Queirós
eca.bio: Eça is the great novelist of 19th-century Portugal. In Os Maias and O Primo Basílio he shows Lisbon society with humour and irony. He worked as a diplomat in Cuba, England and France.

cesario.name: Cesário Verde
cesario.bio: Cesário Verde wrote about the streets, shops and workers of Lisbon. He worked in his family's business and died young of tuberculosis. His friends published his poems as a book after his death.

pessoa.name: Fernando Pessoa
pessoa.bio: Pessoa wrote under many names, called heteronyms: Alberto Caeiro, Ricardo Reis and Álvaro de Campos each have their own life and style. He grew up partly in South Africa and worked in Lisbon as a translator of business letters. Most of his work was found in a trunk after his death.

sacarneiro.name: Mário de Sá-Carneiro
sacarneiro.bio: Sá-Carneiro was a close friend of Fernando Pessoa and one of the young modernists of the magazine Orpheu. He lived in Paris, where he died at the age of 25.

florbela.name: Florbela Espanca
florbela.bio: Florbela Espanca wrote sonnets about love, longing and the wish to be free. She was one of the first women to study law at the University of Lisbon. Many of her poems are sung today.

machado.name: Machado de Assis
machado.bio: Machado de Assis is Brazil's best-known writer. He grew up poor, taught himself and founded the Brazilian Academy of Letters. His novels are full of irony. His Portuguese is Brazilian, of the 19th century.

bilac.name: Olavo Bilac
bilac.bio: Bilac was a Brazilian poet and journalist. He wrote polished, classical verse and the words of the Brazilian flag anthem. His sonnet about the Portuguese language is known in every Portuguese-speaking country.

quotes.author: pessoa
quotes.text: Tudo vale a pena / Se a alma não é pequena.
quotes.meaning: Everything is worth the effort if your soul is not small: big goals are worth their price if you think big.

words.hint: the part of a person that feels and thinks; the soul

quotes.author: camoes
quotes.text: Amor é fogo que arde sem se ver; / É ferida que dói, e não se sente
quotes.source: Rimas, sonnet “Amor é fogo que arde sem se ver”
quotes.meaning: Love is a fire that burns but you cannot see it, a wound that hurts but you do not feel it. Love is full of contradictions.

words.hint: a place where the skin is hurt

quotes.author: machado
quotes.text: Ao vencedor, as batatas!
quotes.meaning: The potatoes go to the winner. In the novel this is an ironic rule of life: the strong take what there is.

words.hint: a vegetable that grows in the ground

quotes.author: pessoa
quotes.text: O Tejo é mais belo que o rio que corre pela minha aldeia, / Mas o Tejo não é mais belo que o rio que corre pela minha aldeia / Porque o Tejo não é o rio que corre pela minha aldeia.
quotes.source: Alberto Caeiro, O Guardador de Rebanhos, XX
quotes.meaning: The Tagus is a more beautiful river, but the small river of your own village means more to you, because it is yours.

words.hint: water that flows to the sea
a very small town in the country
to run; for water: to flow

quotes.author: camoes
quotes.text: As armas e os barões assinalados / Que da ocidental praia Lusitana / Por mares nunca de antes navegados / Passaram ainda além da Taprobana
quotes.meaning: The first lines of Portugal's national epic: the poet will sing of the famous men who sailed from Portugal's western coast over seas nobody had sailed before, even beyond Ceylon (Taprobana).

words.hint: the salt water between the lands
the sand by the sea; here: the coast

quotes.author: pessoa
quotes.text: Não sou nada. / Nunca serei nada. / Não posso querer ser nada. / À parte isso, tenho em mim todos os sonhos do mundo.
quotes.meaning: I am nothing and will never be anything. But apart from that, I have all the dreams of the world inside me.

words.hint: pictures in your head when you sleep; a wish for the future
the earth and all the people on it

quotes.author: bilac
quotes.text: Última flor do Lácio, inculta e bela, / És, a um tempo, esplendor e sepultura
quotes.meaning: Portuguese is the last flower of Latium, the last language born from Latin: wild and beautiful, both something splendid and a grave.

words.hint: the coloured part of a plant
very nice to look at; feminine bela
the place where a dead person lies

quotes.author: garrett
quotes.text: Não te amo, quero-te: o amar vem d'alma.
quotes.meaning: I do not love you, I want you. The speaker says real love comes from the soul, and what he feels is desire.

words.hint: to want; also to love someone

quotes.author: pessoa
quotes.text: Minha pátria é a língua portuguesa.
quotes.meaning: My home country is the Portuguese language. For the writer, the language is the place he belongs to.

words.hint: a language; also the tongue in your mouth

quotes.author: antero
quotes.text: Na mão de Deus, na sua mão direita, / Descansou afinal meu coração.
quotes.meaning: In God's right hand, my heart has found rest at last. After a life of doubt, the poet feels peace.

words.hint: the part at the end of your arm; feminine although it ends in -o
the organ that pumps blood; also feelings

quotes.author: pessoa
quotes.text: O poeta é um fingidor. / Finge tão completamente / Que chega a fingir que é dor / A dor que deveras sente.
quotes.meaning: A poet pretends. He pretends so well that he even pretends that the pain he really feels is pain.

words.hint: a person who writes poems; ends in -a but takes o
what you feel when something hurts

quotes.author: camilo
quotes.text: Amou, perdeu-se e morreu amando.
quotes.meaning: He loved, he was lost, and he died still loving. The narrator sums up the life of his uncle Simão in one line.

words.hint: to lose yourself; to be ruined

quotes.author: camoes
quotes.text: Mudam-se os tempos, mudam-se as vontades, / Muda-se o ser, muda-se a confiança
quotes.source: Rimas, sonnet “Mudam-se os tempos, mudam-se as vontades”
quotes.meaning: Times change, and so do people's wishes, what they are and whom they trust. Nothing stays the same.

words.hint: to change; mudar-se also means to move house
the feeling that you can believe in someone

quotes.author: cesario
quotes.text: Nas nossas ruas, ao anoitecer, / Há tal soturnidade, há tal melancolia
quotes.meaning: In our streets, when night falls, there is such gloom and such sadness. The poet walks through Lisbon at dusk.

words.hint: to get dark in the evening; ao anoitecer = at nightfall

quotes.author: florbela
quotes.text: Ser poeta é ser mais alto, é ser maior / Do que os homens!
quotes.meaning: Being a poet means being taller and greater than other people. The poem says a poet feels more than others.

quotes.author: pessoa
quotes.text: Deus quer, o homem sonha, a obra nasce.
quotes.meaning: God wants it, a person dreams it, and the work is born. Great things start with a wish and a dream.

words.hint: something made: a work; obras are also building works

quotes.author: machado
quotes.text: Não tive filhos, não transmiti a nenhuma criatura o legado da nossa miséria.
quotes.source: Memórias Póstumas de Brás Cubas, last chapter
quotes.meaning: I had no children, so I passed on our human misery to nobody. The dead narrator ends his book with dark humour.

words.hint: what you leave to people after your death

quotes.author: sacarneiro
quotes.text: Perdi-me dentro de mim / Porque eu era labirinto
quotes.meaning: I got lost inside myself, because I was a maze. The poet cannot find his way in his own mind.

words.hint: a place with many paths where you get lost

quotes.author: vieira
quotes.text: Vós, diz Cristo, Senhor nosso, falando com os pregadores, sois o sal da terra
quotes.source: Sermão de Santo António aos Peixes
quotes.meaning: The sermon begins with Christ's words to preachers: you are the salt of the earth. Salt keeps things good, and preachers should keep people good.

words.hint: the white powder that makes food salty
the ground; the earth; also a person's home town

quotes.author: camoes
quotes.text: Onde a terra se acaba e o mar começa
quotes.meaning: Portugal is where the land ends and the sea begins: the western edge of Europe.

quotes.author: pessoa
quotes.text: Para ser grande, sê inteiro: nada / Teu exagera ou exclui. / Sê todo em cada coisa. Põe quanto és / No mínimo que fazes.
quotes.meaning: To be great, be whole: do not make any part of you too big or leave any part out. Put all of yourself into even the smallest thing you do.

quotes.author: eca
quotes.text: Falhámos a vida, menino!
quotes.meaning: We have wasted our lives, my friend! Near the end of the novel, Ega says this to Carlos as they walk through Lisbon.

words.hint: the time from birth to death
a boy; here a friendly way to address a friend

quotes.author: camoes
quotes.text: Erros meus, má fortuna, amor ardente / Em minha perdição se conjuraram
quotes.source: Rimas, sonnet “Erros meus, má fortuna, amor ardente”
quotes.meaning: My mistakes, bad luck and burning love all worked together to ruin me.

words.hint: luck; also a lot of money

quotes.author: pessoa
quotes.text: Sou um guardador de rebanhos. / O rebanho é os meus pensamentos / E os meus pensamentos são todos sensações.
quotes.source: Alberto Caeiro, O Guardador de Rebanhos, IX
quotes.meaning: I am a shepherd, and my flock is my thoughts. My thoughts are all things I feel with my senses.

words.hint: a group of sheep or goats
what you feel through the body

quotes.author: florbela
quotes.text: Minh'alma, de sonhar-te, anda perdida.
quotes.meaning: My soul is lost from dreaming of you. The speaker thinks only of the person she loves.

words.hint: to dream; sonhar-te = to dream of you
to walk; anda perdida = is lost

quotes.author: bilac
quotes.text: Ora (direis) ouvir estrelas!
quotes.meaning: “Come on,” you will say, “listening to the stars!” The poet answers that only someone in love can hear them.

words.hint: a light in the night sky

quotes.author: sacarneiro
quotes.text: Eu não sou eu nem sou o outro, / Sou qualquer coisa de intermédio
quotes.meaning: I am not myself and not the other person either; I am something in between.

words.hint: another one; o outro = the other one

quotes.author: pessoa
quotes.text: Todas as cartas de amor são / Ridículas.
quotes.source: Álvaro de Campos, “Todas as cartas de amor são ridículas”
quotes.meaning: All love letters are silly. The poem goes on to say that people who never wrote one are the really silly ones.

words.hint: a letter you send by post
silly, makes people laugh; feminine ridícula

quotes.author: pessoa
quotes.text: Ó mar salgado, quanto do teu sal / São lágrimas de Portugal!
quotes.meaning: Salty sea, how much of your salt is the tears of Portugal! The voyages cost many lives and much sorrow.

words.hint: a drop of water from your eye when you cry
the white powder that makes food salty

quotes.author: machado
quotes.text: Ao verme que primeiro roeu as frias carnes do meu cadáver dedico como saudosa lembrança estas memórias póstumas.
quotes.source: Memórias Póstumas de Brás Cubas, dedication
quotes.meaning: The dead narrator dedicates his book to the first worm that ate his cold body. The novel starts with a joke about death.

words.hint: a small animal without legs that lives in the ground
to offer a book to someone
